newsitem.title: USA: NY Assembly to weigh its plan for big school bond.
newsitem.headline: NY Assembly to weigh its plan for big school bond.

text.p: The New York State Assembly will consider on Wednesday its plan for a $2 billion school bond that would raise funds to rebuild and modernize the state's public schools.

Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, said in a statement, "Through this bond initiative, we provide the resources to sweep away the cramped and crumbling schools that are obstacles to educational excellence and clear pathways to success for futures generations."
Silver said he was confident that if placed on the November ballot, the bond measure would be approved by voters.
Pataki has blasted the Assembly for wanting to spend too much in its own plan for a fiscal 1998 budget, though the body has forecast bigger revenues than the Republican governor.

In his own budget, Pataki has proposed a five-year plan he says would give homeowners $1.8 billion of direct property tax relief and $1.7 billion of additional aid for public schools. State funding for children's education would rise $302 million in fiscal 1998 and $2 billion over five years.

The Assembly lawmakers noted that New York City's schools have 10 percent or 91,000 students more than they have room for, while the average age of its schools was 57 years. Other cities also have old schools: Buffalo's average was 65 years.
The plan for a $2 billion bond--which would be bigger than the $1.75 billion Clean Water/Clean Air bond approved by the voters last November, is part of a three-prong plan to aid the state's schools.

The Democrat-led Assembly also wants to raise state building aid reimbursement by 50 percent and create a $250 million fund to help districts pay for minor maintenance and repairs, if local voters approve them.

Calling upon the Senate, which is controlled by Republicans, to put forward its views on education, Silver noted the Assembly's school bond would create jobs. The proposed bond act would let districts ask for funding to pay for up to 100 percent of six kinds of projects:

--new construction, expanding classrooms or buildings, buying or improving real property, like handicapped access, modernization and rehabilitation, environmental rehabiliation, like asbestos removal, and wiring needed to use computers.
